Kızılcık Şerbeti dizisinde hayat verdiği Pembe karakteriyle hafızalara kazınan Sibel Taşçıoğlu, diziden ayrılık süreci hakkında ilk kez açıklama yaptı. Karavanında yaşandığı öne sürülen olayla ilgili kendisine atfedilen sözlerin gerçeği yansıtmadığını belirten oyuncu, ayrılığının kendi tercihi olmadığını söyledi.
Sibel Taşçıoğlu'nun Kızılcık Şerbeti'nden ayrılığı sonrası ortaya atılan iddialarda, oyuncunun karavanında insan dışkısı bulunduğu ve bu olayın sorumluluğunu üstlenmek zorunda kaldığı öne sürülmüştü.
Söz konusu iddiaların yeniden gündeme gelmesi üzerine sessizliğini bozan Taşçıoğlu, kendisine atfedilen açıklamaların hiçbir zaman yapılmadığını belirtti.
“Son günlerde Kızılcık Şerbeti dizisinden ayrılışımla ilgili, şahsıma atfedilen ve gerçekle hiçbir ilgisi olmayan açıklamaların yeniden gündeme getirildiğini görüyorum. Öncelikle belirtmek isterim ki söz konusu ifadeler bana ait değildir. Böyle bir açıklamam ya da röportajım olmamıştır. Bugüne kadar diziden ayrılış sürecimle ilgili konuşmamayı tercih ettim. Çünkü yaşananların kamuoyu önünde bir tartışmaya dönüşmesini doğru bulmadım. Ancak sessizliğimin gerçek dışı hikâyelerle doldurulmasını da artık kabul etmiyorum.”
Diziden ayrılışının kendi kararı olmadığını açıkça dile getiren Taşçıoğlu, sürecin arkasında çalışma ortamında yaşanan bazı anlaşmazlıkların bulunduğunu ifade etti.
“Kızılcık Şerbeti dizisinden ayrılmak benim tercihim değildi. Ayrılığımın arkasında, çalışma sürecinde yaşanan ve mesleki duruşum gereği sessiz kalmayı tercih etmediğim bazı anlaşmazlıklar vardı. Bu konuların ayrıntılarına bugün de girmeyi gerekli görmüyorum.
Öte yandan, başka bir oyuncuyu küçük düşüren, kişisel ve mahrem konular üzerinden üretilen iddiaların benim adım kullanılarak yayılmasını da son derece yanlış buluyorum. Hiç kimsenin itibarlarının bu şekilde zedelenmesini doğru bulmadım, bugün de bulmuyorum.”
Kendisine ait olmayan sözlerin haberleştirilmesine de tepki gösteren Sibel Taşçıoğlu, gazeteciliğin doğrulanmış bilgileri aktarmak olduğunu vurguladı.
“Gazeteciliğin temel sorumluluğu, duyulanı değil doğrulananı kamuoyuyla paylaşmaktır. Hiçbir araştırma yapılmadan, kaynağı sorgulanmadan, bir insanın ağzından söylenmemiş sözlerin aktarılmasını habercilik olarak görmüyorum. Gerçek dışı içeriklerin daha fazla ilgi ve etkileşim uğruna yayılmasını kabul etmiyor, bu yayınları yapanları sorumlulukla hareket etmeye davet ediyorum.
Bugüne kadar sessiz kalmamın nedeni söyleyecek sözümün olmaması değil, mesleğime ve birlikte çalıştığım insanlara duyduğum saygıydı.
Ancak saygıyla susmak, gerçeğin çarpıtılmasını kabul etmek değildir.

ABD'li çip üreticisi Intel 'e, kişisel bilgisayar (PC) pazarındaki yavaşlamanın ve tedarik sorunlarının şirket gelirlerine etkisini yatırımcılardan gizlediği ve yanıltıcı açıklamalarda bulunduğu iddiasıyla toplu dava açıldı.
Southfield İtfaiye ve Polis Emeklilik Sistemi'nin öncülüğünde açılan davada, Intel Üst Yöneticisi (CEO) Lip-Bu Tan ve Finans Direktörü (CFO) David Zinsner de davalılar arasında yer aldı.
California Kuzey Bölge Mahkemesi'ne sunulan dava dilekçesinde, Intel'in 23 Temmuz-29 Ekim 2026 döneminde şirketin adi hisselerini satın alan yatırımcıları yanıltıcı açıklamalarla zarara uğrattığı öne sürüldü.
Dilekçeye göre şirket yöneticileri, yapay zeka kaynaklı talep artışının ve veri merkezlerine yönelik sunucu işlemcisi satışlarının Intel'in büyümesini desteklediğini belirten olumlu açıklamalar yaptı. Buna karşılık, yöneticilerin PC pazarındaki yavaşlamanın boyutunu, iş ortaklarında biriken ihtiyaç fazlası stokları ve üretimi sınırlayan tedarik sorunlarını yatırımcılara açıklamadığı iddia edildi.
Dilekçede ayrıca Intel'in 12 Ağustos'ta hisse başına 95 dolardan 240 milyondan fazla hisse satarak yaklaşık 23 milyar dolar brüt gelir elde ettiği belirtildi. Davacı taraf, bu işlemin davalıların yatırımcıları yanıltmak için gerekçeye ve fırsata sahip olduğu yönündeki iddiasını desteklediğini öne sürdü.
Davacı taraf, mahkemeden davanın toplu dava olarak görülmesini ve yatırımcıların zararlarının tazmin edilmesini istedi.
Intel, 29 Ekim'de açıkladığı 2026'nın üçüncü çeyrek sonuçlarında, PC faaliyetlerini kapsayan İstemci Bilişim ve Fiziksel Yapay Zeka Grubu'nun (CCPG) gelirinin geçen yılın aynı dönemine göre yüzde 5 azalarak 8,1 milyar dolara gerilediğini bildirmişti.
Şirketin dördüncü çeyrek için açıkladığı 15-16 milyar dolarlık gelir beklentisi ve hisse başına 25 sentlik kâr öngörüsü, analistlerin tahminlerinin altında kalmıştı.
Intel hisseleri, 29 Ekim'de 92,07 dolardan kapanmış, 30 Ekim'de ise yüzde 28,6 değer kaybederek 65,76 dolara gerilemişti. Düşüş, şirketin piyasa değerinden yaklaşık 140 milyar dolar silmişti.

Bank of America, Chase, US Bank, Wells Fargo and Truist were listed by users who have been experiencing issues
Customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
Chase said the technical problems were not a systemic issue and were not the result of a cyber-attack, and that it was working to bring banking services back online.
“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”
The disruption comes after a major outage by Microsoft that began on Thursday and lasted into the next day, which crippled a host of services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. The outage had serious repercussions for millions of people and organizations all over the world, including schools, hospitals, businesses, courts, banks, prisons, police forces and governments.
Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The office software giant did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, identifying in an initial report on Monday that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity sparked the outage.
Also on Friday, ageing equipment led to a temporary grounding of all commercial airplanes in the US, sparking travel chaos as thousands of flights were delayed or canceled. The Trump administration later said the four-hour ground stop stemmed from routine maintenance.
At a briefing on Saturday, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said the outage began after “a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire … to fiber” and a newly installed router “started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system”.
The FAA, he said, was still working to determine whether the fault was “incompetence” by the contractor, or “a faulty router”.
Monday’s technical issues seem to center on Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, including Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services.
A spokesman for US Bank said its systems are not directly affected but that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
Zelle, the peer-to-peer payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money near-instantly to friends and family, is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo .
A spokesperson for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational. “An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,” they said.
Some Chase customers received a message that said: “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”

Hissedarlar, kişisel bilgisayar satışlarındaki durgunluğun şirketin sonuçlarını ne kadar olumsuz etkilediğini gizlediği iddiasıyla ABD'li çip üreticisi Intel'e dava açtı.
Şirket, PC pazarındaki durgunluğu ve üretim darboğazlarını gerekçe göstererek dördüncü çeyrek için beklenenden daha zayıf bir gelir tahmini yayımlamasının ardından, 30 Ekim'de Intel hisseleri yaklaşık yüzde 29 düştü.
İtfaiyeciler ve polis memurları için bir Michigan emeklilik fonu olan City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, önerilen toplu davayı 13 Kasım Cuma günü açtı. Fonun hukuk bürosu Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd, davayı aynı akşam ABD'de duyurarak büyük kayıpları bulunan yatırımcıları baş davacı olmak için başvurmaya davet etti.
Şikayet dilekçesinde, Intel ve yöneticilerinin şirketin faaliyetleri ve mali durumu hakkında "önemli ölçüde yanlış ve/veya yanıltıcı" açıklamalar yaptığı iddia ediliyor. Dilekçede, kişisel bilgisayar satışlarındaki zayıflığın, dizüstü ve masaüstü bilgisayar çiplerini kapsayan Client Computing ve Physical AI Group bölümünü ne kadar olumsuz etkilediğinin Intel tarafından olduğundan az gösterildiği öne sürülüyor.
Intel, daha geniş PC pazarının zayıfladığını önceden uyarmıştı. Ancak temmuz ayındaki bilanço telekonferansında Mali İşler Direktörü David Zinsner, dizüstü ve masaüstü bilgisayar çiplerinden elde edilen gelirin üçüncü çeyrekte kabaca sabit kalmasını, bölümün genel gelirinin ise hafif artmasını beklediğini söyledi.
Intel 29 Ekim'de üçüncü çeyrek sonuçlarını açıkladığında, bölümün geliri önceki çeyreğe göre yüzde 9 düşmüştü ve yaklaşık 800 milyon dolar (719 milyon euro) azalarak 8,1 milyar dolara (7,3 milyar euro) gerilemişti.
Intel'in üç aylık raporu, dizüstü ve masaüstü bilgisayar gelirinin 6,9 milyar dolara (6,2 milyar euro) gerilediğini, bunun bir yıl öncesine göre 424 milyon dolar (381 milyon euro) düşüş anlamına geldiğini ortaya koydu. Şirket, zayıflayan talep ve rekabet nedeniyle satılan birim sayısının yüzde 14 daha az olduğunu bildirdi.
Dizüstü ve masaüstü bilgisayar üreticileri bir süredir bellek çiplerindeki arz sıkıntıları ve yükselen bileşen maliyetleriyle mücadele ediyor. Üreticilerin parça tedarikinde zorlanması ve yükselen fiyatların alıcıları caydırması nedeniyle PC sevkiyatları azalmış durumda.
Intel ekim ayında, müşterilerin stoklarını azaltmak için siparişleri kısmaya başladığını söylemişti. Dava dilekçesinde, bileşen maliyetlerindeki artışın fiyatları yükseltmesiyle PC üreticileri ve distribütörlerinin satılamayan bilgisayarlardan oluşan büyük stoklarla baş başa kaldığı iddia ediliyor.
Intel ayrıca sunucu çiplerine yönelik talebi tam olarak karşılayamadığını, bunun da yapay zeka veri merkezlerinin genişlemesinden ne ölçüde yararlanabileceğini sınırladığını belirtti.
Intel, dördüncü çeyrek gelirinin 15 ila 16 milyar dolar (13,5 ila 14,4 milyar euro) arasında olacağını öngördü. Tahminin orta noktası, şirketin üçüncü çeyrek gelirinden 1 milyar dolar (900 milyon euro) daha düşük ve şikayet dilekçesine göre ortalama analist tahmininin yaklaşık 1,5 milyar dolar (1,35 milyar euro) altında kaldı.
Şirket, PC pazarındaki durgunluğun en az 2027'nin ilk yarısına kadar sürmesini bekliyor. Birim bazında ölçüldüğünde, genel PC pazarının 2026'daki yaklaşık yüzde 12'lik daralmanın ardından 2027'de yaklaşık yüzde 10 küçüleceğini öngörüyor.
Intel, ürünlerine yönelik daha uzun vadeli talep konusunda iyimserliğini koruyor, üretimi artırmak için daha fazla ekipman sipariş ediyor.
Intel sonuçlarını açıklamadan önce, 29 Ekim borsa kapanışına gelindiğinde şirketin hisseleri 2025 sonundan bu yana iki kattan fazla artmıştı. Yatırımcılar, şirketin yapay zeka patlamasından fayda sağlayacağına oynuyordu. Intel, yapay zekanın giderek daha yaygın kullanılmasıyla genel amaçlı sunucu çiplerine olan talebin arttığını söylüyor.

OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office , alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security pose an ongoing danger to the public.
At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident , OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.”
The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients.
The complaint centers on the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems , DseWiki , the Wikimedia Foundation , and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing.
The complaint also alleges that dozens of similar incidents have occurred without public disclosure.
“OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.”
The central allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices constitute a public nuisance because the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public. A secondary claim alleges unfair competition stemming from the marketing of an unsafe product. If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI could face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court.
It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states. In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users , particularly children and teenagers. In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe into deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed.
In a statement to the press, California Attorney General Rob Bonta presented the case as an effort to maintain public safety in the face of a powerful new technology.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in the statement. “The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.”
In a statement, OpenAI emphasized the company’s extensive effort to investigate the Hugging Face incident and improve its systems in the aftermath.
“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI said. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

Attorney General Rob Bonta says Hugging Face attack was ‘entirely predictable’ result of emphasis on rapid growth.
California has filed a lawsuit against the technology firm OpenAI, alleging that the company endangered the public by developing an artificial intelligence model without the appropriate safeguards.
The lawsuit, announced by Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday, centres on an incident that unfolded in July, when one of OpenAI’s experimental models gained access to the internet.
It proceeded to launch a days-long cyberattack on the AI hosting platform Hugging Face .
In the California complaint, Bonta argues that the incident indicates that OpenAI pursues growth over guardrails, leading to potentially dangerous errors.
“The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritises growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement.
The lawsuit is the first brought by a state in response to the July incident. It alleges that OpenAI violated California’s consumer protection laws and created a public nuisance through its actions.
The complaint, filed in a state court in San Francisco, calls for civil penalties against OpenAI and an injunction to bar it from engaging in actions that constitute “unfair competition”.
“The simple truth is that the attack was entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s decision to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight,” the complaint reads.
The Hugging Face incident became a catalyst for anxieties in the US about the explosive growth of the AI industry and the relatively light oversight it receives from the government.
President Donald Trump’s administration has largely opposed blanket regulations on the AI industry, warning that such rules could stifle the industry’s growth.
In December 2025, for instance, Trump issued an executive order attempting to limit the ability of individual states to pass laws that might govern AI development.
“United States AI companies must be free to innovate without cumbersome regulation. But excessive State regulation thwarts this imperative,” the order reads.
“My Administration must act with the Congress to ensure that there is a minimally burdensome national standard — not 50 discordant State ones.”
Polls, however, show that a majority of Americans want to see greater oversight of AI development and are wary that the technology could fuel economic and social disruptions.
The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, for instance, found in October that 64 percent of US adults believe AI is developing too rapidly. Roughly 81 percent said the technology should be kept under human control, rather than be left to operate independently.
Several high-profile resignations in the AI sector — notably that of Jacob Coxon in September — have also spurred concerns about the lack of oversight.
“They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon, formerly a researcher at the AI firm Anthropic, wrote in a social media post about his departure.
“Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.”
In Monday’s lawsuit, California officials accuse companies like OpenAI of failing to “adequately secure and monitor” their AI tests. It also alleged that the company had obstructed state investigators when they attempted to look into incidents like the Hugging Face hacking.
“OpenAI thwarted the Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit said.
OpenAI has responded to July’s incident by stating that it would reinforce its safety measures and acknowledging the need for greater transparency.
In September, it also published a framework for “tracking, investigating, and disclosing instances of model misalignment” to better inform lawmakers and the public.

texts.https://www.wired.com/story/jpmorganchas:
Customers of many major financial institutions experienced unspecified technical issues on Monday as thousands of reports flooded the uptime-tracking website Downdetector.com from people saying that they had issues using their banks in some way.
It is currently unclear which systems are having issues. However, the problem may stem from technical difficulties at JPMorganChase, the top retail bank that holds over 10 percent of all US deposits, did identify a specific issue.
“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems—there is no evidence this is cyber-related,” says JPMorganChase spokesperson Pablo Rodriguez. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”
Rodriguez adds that the bank is not experiencing a “systemic issue” but that “other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.” The spokesperson adds that customers “still have access to their accounts and funds” and that the bank is working to resolve the issues.
Apparent issues with the banks, credit unions, fintech apps, and credit card companies appear to begin around 9:30 am ET and peaked at around 2 pm ET. Many people also reported issues using Zelle , the peer-to-peer money-transfer system adopted by major banks. However, in a statement, Zelle denied its systems were the cause of the reported outages while acknowledging that issues at banks may impact people’s ability to use Zelle.
“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” a Zelle spokesperson says in a statement. “Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds.”
US Bank spokesperson Jeffrey Shelman also says the financial institution’s systems “are not directly impacted.” Shelman adds, however, that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
Seth Eisen, senior vice president of communications at MasterCard, says, “Our network is operating normally.” A Visa spokesperson says the company is aware of the ongoing payments issue, but that Visa’s systems are operating normally too.
According to reports on Downdetector, which is sourced to user reports rather than official statements, the issues on Monday also impacted customers of Bank of America, Capital One, Wells Fargo, TD Bank, Navy Credit Federal Union, and more. These companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Eisen, the Mastercard VP, says that DownDetector was “not correct” in the case of his company.
Whatever the cause, the timing of the issues may as well have been designed to get people looking for broader patterns. Last Thursday, Microsoft 365 experienced an unprecedented 24-hour outage that impacted millions of people, governments, businesses, and other institutions globally. Microsoft executive vice president Charles Lamanna said in a post on X on Monday that the outage, which impacted Outlook, Teams, and many other Microsoft cloud services, was related to an update that started rolling out in July but only began causing problems last week.
Soon after Microsoft resolved its outage on Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop order. This time, the issue was related to a problem with Air Traffic Control’s communications systems. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” the agency wrote in an FAQ explaining the outage. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”
The FAA’s five-hour ground stop resulted in thousands of canceled flights and otherwise disrupted travel for countless travelers. The impact of Monday’s banking outage remains unclear.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c574:
Robert Pattinson has starred in films including the Twilight franchise and The Batman
Robert Pattinson's career is already flying high with roles in films including the Twilight series, The Batman and The Odyssey, so signing up to play James Bond will propel his profile into the stratosphere.
He's already established himself as a leading man, action star and character actor, which is clearly why he is about to play the suave, British secret agent 007.
At 40, he is slightly older than some of the other men reportedly lined up for the role , but he's also the most famous - something the new Bond studio Amazon-MGM may have favoured, with an eye on the box office.
His recent work has garnered both critical and box office success, including Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster The Odyssey, in which he played the villainous Antinous.
Pattinson was also called "Oscar-worthy" by the Independent and "superb" by The Times, for his performance in November's Primetime, as the real-life host of US TV show To Catch a Predator.
He also helped lead 2022's The Batman to the second-biggest North American opening of the Covid-19 pandemic behind Spider-Man: No Way Home. The Guardian said he played the "brooding" role with " appealing vulnerability , external ".
Meanwhile in dark romantic comedy The Drama, he and his co-star gave a "career-highlight performance" , external . It's one of three films he appeared in with Zendaya this year, along with The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three.
Robert Pattinson starred in 2022's The Batman, which was described by critics as a grim, gritty, and gripping super-noir
Born in Barnes, south-west London, Pattinson grew up with his father, a classic car trader and mother, who worked at a modelling agency, and two elder sisters.
His interest in acting started while he was still at school, when he joined the Barnes Theatre Club.
"I wouldn't be acting if it wasn't for that little club," he told Your Local Guardian in 2008 , external .
"I went originally because a lot of pretty girls went there," he said. "I worked backstage and I started acting when all the good people left and I was the only one tall enough to play the lead.
"In a weird sort of way, that stuff was probably the best I've done and the stuff I am most proud of."
He landed his first big film role more than two decades ago, playing Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. A relatively minor character, but it was enough to get him noticed.
Robert Pattinson and Kristen Stewart starred in five Twilight films from 2005 to 2012
Three years later, he had a starring role in the first of five Twilight films, along with Kristen Stewart, in which they played star-crossed lovers - vampire Edward Cullen and mortal-turned vampire Kristen Stewart.
Based on Stephanie Meyer's hugely popular young adult books, the films globally grossed more than $3bn (£2.2bn) by 2012, and established Pattinson as a heartthrob.
He spoke in his early career of finding his often adoring, screaming fans hard to deal with.
"Although is part of the job, it feels like they have been paid to turn up and scream at me at 7.30pm," he said.
"Nothing I don't think can prepare you for the fans. I don't know why I'm not getting used to it but I'm completely overwhelmed every time."
In 2010, Time included him in their list of 100 people who "most affect our world" , external , saying perhaps prophetically that "we haven't seen a tenth of what he can do on screen".
After such mainstream success with the Twilight franchise, Pattinson was able to branch out.
He went on to work with several acclaimed independent film directors including David Cronenberg, starring in his film Cosmpopolis in 2012, as well as working with Werner Herzog in 2015's Queen of the Desert and The Lighthouse (2019), directed by Robert Eggers.
Pattinson told Screen Daily why he took the role in psychological horror film The Lighthouse , external , saying he told Eggers: "I just want to do something weird."
Pattinson and Zendaya have appeared in three films together this year - The Drama, The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three
The following year though, he was back in big-studio territory, with Odyssey director Christopher Nolan, in sci-fi thriller Tenet, and again in 2022 with The Batman, directed by Matt Reeves and co-starring Zoe Kravitz and Paul Dano.
Pattinson told Screen Daily why he returned to big-budget films, explaining: "I guess I was trying to do the opposite of what I've been doing. I started thinking, 'I really want to do a big thing.'
"I hadn't done something with a massive budget for ages. But you approach it exactly the same way."
The Batman got generally positive reviews, re-establishing Pattinson with a broader range of fans.
By 2025, when he was on the red carpet for Parasite director Bong Joon Ho's sci-fi black comedy, Mickey 17, he said it was "quite strange" to have a fanbase that was now dominated by men , external .
"There's like a bunch of guys, which is a new one for me!" he told the Associated Press.
Pattinson's private life has often created interest in the press, not least his previous relationships with Stewart, and then the singer FKA Twigs.
Since 2018, he has been in a relationship with model Suki Waterhouse. They got engaged in December 2023 and had their first child, a daughter, in March.
Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse have been a couple since 2018
With his latest role as James Bond, Pattinson will be extremely busy, not least because the forthcoming Batman sequel is reportedly due out in 2028.
But the actor will have a head start as 007, having already worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve, who also helmed Dune: Part Three.
Pattinson was full of praise for him on their most recent film, despite the strain of working in the furnace-like heat of the desert.
"The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own Dune theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all," he told the New York Times , external .
"There are no negatives. Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them.
"He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress."
Sounds like Pattinson will have the cool head needed to juggle his forthcoming roles - including James Bond. You could even say he may end up being shaken, but not stirred.

Airline executives support modernising FAA systems as US Transportation Secretary Duffy seeks $50bn from Congress for FAA overhaul.
Following the nationwide ground stop last week , United States airlines could face a financial hit of hundreds of millions of dollars even as airline executives press for increased investment in ageing air traffic control infrastructure .
The four largest US airlines – American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines – could face a combined hit of $345m to pretax earnings, according to brokerage firm Bernstein.
The effects of Friday’s ground stop continued to ripple through airline schedules on Monday, with more than 18,500 flights within, into or out of the US cancelled since the disruption began, according to FlightAware data.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC on Monday that the wider impact of the disruption could run into the “billions of dollars”. No official estimate of the total economic cost has been released yet.
Flights were grounded across the country for more than four hours on Friday, and the disruption continued to affect airline schedules over the weekend.
Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian also said the financial impact could run into the “billions”, telling Fortune on Monday that the disruption underscored the need for greater investment in the country’s air traffic control infrastructure.
Bastian pointed to the vast sums investors are putting into artificial intelligence and data centres, adding that the US should also be investing in its aviation system.
United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby agreed that the disruption should be a “call to action”, saying the air traffic control system needed greater investment in modern technology to improve its reliability.
Transportation Secretary Duffy has asked US Congress for $50bn for air traffic control and airport infrastructure upgrades, an addition to the $12.5bn lawmakers approved for air traffic control modernisation last year.
The existing system relies on outdated equipment and needs a comprehensive overhaul, he said.
But Democrats have questioned the request, saying only about $1bn of the $12.5bn already approved has been spent so far.
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump called on Congress to approve the funding, arguing that the upgrades should be carried out all at once rather than in stages.
“We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The funding debate is moving into a narrow window for congressional action. The House and Senate are scheduled to convene once more before the end of the year.
Speaker Mike Johnson has said lawmakers will take up the administration’s funding request during the current Congress’s lame-duck session, but Democrats have demanded more information on how the money will be spent.
The precise cause of Friday’s failure remains under investigation. Duffy has said the problem began at a remote Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) site in Arkansas where workers from defence contractor L3Harris were replacing ageing copper wiring with fibre-optic cables.
The Government Accountability Office, the congressional watchdog, raised concerns about the FAA’s management of its modernisation programme in a September report. It found that the agency had not developed an integrated schedule for the first phase of upgrades, and warned that poor planning increased the risk of disrupting air traffic control operations.

The lawsuit stems from an earlier incident where the tech company’s products hacked into the open-source platform Hugging Face
California sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the artificial intelligence titan of developing its technology without safety or the public’s interest in mind.
The lawsuit concerns an incident earlier this year where OpenAI agents – semi-autonomous AI software that can carry out digital actions on behalf of users – launched a cyber-attack into the open-source AI platform Hugging Face.
Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, said the “infamous” attack was just one of 80 known incidents involving “loss of control” and shows that OpenAI doesn’t have adequate safeguards in place to protect society.
“While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability,” Bonta said in a statement.
The lawsuit, filed in state superior court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California’s Unfair Competition Law and is a public nuisance as defined by state law. Bonta is asking the court to order OpenAI to change its business practices and pay civil penalties.
California’s lawsuit follows Bonta’s formal investigation into OpenAI, launched in September, over the Hugging Face incident, followed by a subpoena of the company probing other cybersecurity incidents and risks with its models. The Federal Trade Commission is also conducting an industry-wide investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI labs over the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers’ digital security.
In July, OpenAI revealed that one of its autonomous AI agents went rogue during a test , accessing the open web and hacking into Hugging Face. The company called it an “unprecedented cyber-incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities”.
Since then, several other incidents involving OpenAI have come to light, including a breach of government websites in Australia. Other AI firms, including Anthropic and Google, have also disclosed rogue agent activity .
Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company has worked to create safeguards for its AI models, along with identifying and disclosing incidents of “misalignment”. He said most cases identified have been low severity with limited-to-no impact.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” Pusateri said. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.”
During a press conference, Bonta said OpenAI violated the law and that his suit is meant to ensure the company puts proper safeguards in place. He noted that the possibility exists for AI agents to hack into the power grid and medical and financial institutions.
“These risks are no longer hypothetical,” Bonta said. “Without sufficient safeguards and controls, the scope and frequency of this already unacceptable risk will only increase.”

As tech industry pushes for return, US president says he thinks Huang ‘learned a big lesson’
Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, joining Silicon Valley heavyweights in backing the reinstatement of the AI figurehead.
The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back.
“I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told ​reporters as he left the ‌White House on ‌a trip to Asia. “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return.”
The comments came as the US government announced a crackdown on companies such as Nvidia selling AI chips and servers to overseas datacentres that in turn are supplying computing power to China and other US adversaries.
Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, and a host of other tech bosses have signed an open letter calling for the reinstatement of Huang.
The reinstatement letter has more than 165,000 signatories and demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.
The former Nvidia CEO resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who is no relation. His resignation ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded.
Days earlier, Huang had admitted being unfaithful to his wife without specifying who else was involved.
Trump said on Monday: “Nobody’s proven that [Alice Huang] is a spy. She may not be a spy.” Trump has faced questions after it was reported that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in his administration.
According to the Financial Times , Huang has discussed with people close to him a possible return to the company. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for his return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House. The FT also reported on Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang.
One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Colette Kress , Nvidia’s chief financial officer – the best option.
“We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO, and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”.
The new rule announced by the US government on Monday requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on ⁠them being illegally diverted.
“The rule ‌is designed to ​ensure that ​existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving datacentres in third countries,” the US Department of Commerce said.
Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, worked as an executive at the Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. According to reports, Megaspeed is under suspicion of diverting powerful Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export laws.
Megaspeed said on Sunday it was a “legitimate and lawful business” and that Huang had left the business in late 2025. It added that it complied “with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”.
Nvidia shares closed down 4.1% on Monday, knocking about $160bn (£121bn) off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.76tn compared with $4.5tn before the scandal broke.

Nvidia faces potential 30 percent value loss without Jensen Huang, say market analysts amid stock downturn.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley insiders are calling on chipmaker Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang, who resigned last week from the company he cofounded.
Musk is one of the 177,000 signatories to a petition titled “Stand With Jensen”, calling for the reinstatement of the executive, who resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
“We are current and former NVIDIA employees, partners, shareholders, and supporters. We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA’s best interests,” the letter published on the petition’s website said.
More privately, a group of Silicon Valley insiders is pushing to get Huang back in the role, with the Financial Times reporting that Huang is considering a comeback. The paper reported that an unnamed group of Silicon Valley insiders has put together a so-called war room and is lobbying the White House for support which is a move that may have been successful.
“A lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” United States President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday.
Trump’s reported trades this year suggest he held between $13m and $62m in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, the Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures.
But Nvidia’s board is not considering bringing Jensen back, the Reuters news agency reported citing three unnamed people.
Much of Nvidia’s value is tied to Huang, with analysts estimating that the company could lose as much as 25 to 30 percent of its value without him .
Nvidia’s stock was trending downward in early trading on Wall Street, with US markets opening down 2.3 percent on the day. Over the last five days, the stock has dropped 8.5 percent and is down more than 25.7 percent over the last month.
The developments come as the White House moves to designate Nvidia, along with more than two dozen other companies, as “national champions” in the artificial intelligence industry, a new initiative intended to help the company secure more business overseas, according to reporting by The Wall Street Journal.
They also come as the Trump administration issued a rule on Monday that it would restrict China’s access to chips made by companies including Nvidia, as Trump begins a trip to China where he will meet with President Xi Jinping.
The restrictions are aimed at preventing Chinese companies from “circumventing” existing limits by using data centres in Southeast Asian countries such as Malaysia and Thailand to train their AI models.
“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries,” the Department of Commerce said in a statement.
The new rule comes as the Commerce Department is scrambling to demonstrate that it is cracking down on Chinese access to sensitive US technology, following reports that the agency under Secretary Howard Lutnick turned a blind eye to the smuggling of advanced Nvidia AI chips into China.

Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, backed the effort.
Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, adding to a list of supporters who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.
Fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.
But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in bringing him back after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.
Meanwhile on Monday, the Trump administration said it will further restrict China's ​access to AI chips from companies like Nvidia.
The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance. Since his departure, supporters have launched an online petition demanding his return.
Musk and Sweeny are among the more than 175,000 who have signed the open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.
The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by a make up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".
President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.
"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.
The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models.
The move came ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jingping this week.
The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted to China.
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy. However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.
The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , external , though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.
The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.
President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.
It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China.
"They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that," he said.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.
The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.
"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X. , external
"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."
Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."
But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".
Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.
Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.
In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".
Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
“It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”
Trump went on to contradict previous findings from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy.
“He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did … That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.”
Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims.
The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report.
Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang.
“A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. Referring to the former Apple chief executive, Trump added: “I recommended Tim Cook.”

California Kuzey Bölge Mahkemesine sunulan dava dilekçesinde, Intel'in 23 Temmuz-29 Ekim 2026 döneminde şirketin adi hisse senetlerini satın alan yatırımcıları yanıltıcı açıklamalarla zarara uğrattığı öne sürüldü.
Şirket yöneticilerinin yapay zeka kaynaklı talep artışının ve veri merkezlerine yönelik sunucu işlemcisi satışlarının Intel'in büyümesini desteklediğine ilişkin olumlu açıklamalar yaptığı belirtilen dilekçede, buna karşın PC pazarındaki yavaşlamanın boyutunun, şirketin iş ortaklarında biriken ihtiyaç fazlası stokların ve üretimi kısıtlayan tedarik sorunlarının yatırımcılara açıklanmadığı iddia edildi.
Dilekçede ayrıca, Intel'in 12 Ağustos'ta hisse başına 95 dolardan 240 milyondan fazla hisse satarak yaklaşık 23 milyar dolar brüt gelir elde ettiği ve bu işlemin davalıların yatırımcıları yanıltmak için motivasyon ve fırsata sahip olduğu iddiasını desteklediği öne sürüldü.
AA'nın haberine göre davacı taraf, mahkemeden davanın toplu dava olarak görülmesini ve yatırımcıların zararlarının tazmin edilmesini talep etti.
Intel, 29 Ekim'de açıkladığı 2026'nın üçüncü çeyreğine ilişkin finansal sonuçlarında, PC faaliyetlerini kapsayan İstemci Bilişim ve Fiziksel Yapay Zeka Grubu (CCPG) segmentinin gelirinin yıllık bazda yüzde 5 azalarak 8,1 milyar dolara gerilediğini bildirmişti.
Şirketin dördüncü çeyrek için 15-16 milyar dolar aralığında açıkladığı gelir beklentisi ile hisse başına 25 sentlik kar öngörüsü, analistlerin tahminlerinin altında kalmıştı.
Intel hisseleri, 29 Ekim'de 92,07 dolardan kapanmasının ardından 30 Ekim'de yüzde 28,6 değer kaybederek 65,76 dolara gerilemişti. Söz konusu düşüşle şirketin piyasa değerinden yaklaşık 140 milyar dolar silinmişti. *Haberin fotoğrafı AP tarafından servis edilmiştir.
Zonguldak'ta, 21 Ekim'de çöken binanın olduğu bölgedeki 2 katlı bina kendiliğinden yıkıldı. Binanın çökme anları, çevredekilerin cep telefonuyla görüntülendi. (DHA)

The classifier flagged fewer false positives for humans to review, while getting better at identifying abusive content.
OpenAI is announcing a tool that it says will help child sexual abuse investigators cut through the noise to find harmful material they can act on quickly.
At a Monday press briefing in Washington, DC, OpenAI announced a classifier it says can better detect abusive imagery of kids, including whether it’s AI-generated. It’s also offering free access to vetted organizations, giving developers more guidance on how to detect this type of content, and helping to train law enforcement on how AI can aid their investigations. The news comes as policymakers and others are pushing for more safety restrictions on AI tools, accusing OpenAI and other companies of facilitating harm to children.
In recent years, AI-generated sexual images of children have threatened to overwhelm systems like the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) CyberTipline, which collects and triages reports of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The CyberTipline received 400,000 generative AI-related reports in 2025, an exponential increase from the 67,000 it received in 2024, and researchers have warned that the influx could make NCMEC’s workload “unmanageable.” The US government has stated that both AI-generated and non-AI-generated CSAM is illegal, and 48 states have laws to address sexually explicit AI deepfakes. But the tools to make them are widely available , and researchers say that a flood of fake images can make it harder to tell when a child is actively experiencing harm.
The influx of AI-generated CSAM reports to NCMEC is “explosive”
North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who cochairs the AG Alliance’s AI Task Force , said at OpenAI’s event that the influx of AI-generated CSAM reports to NCMEC is “explosive” — and if they keep going that way, “it is going to mean that we fail in our mission.” Tech companies are facing a range of policy proposals that could require them to take more action against CSAM and other potentially harmful content for kids. The Take It Down Act now requires social media platforms to remove real or AI-generated nonconsensual intimate images within 48 hours, and the newly elected Congress could seek to take stronger action against AI companies like SpaceXSI, whose Grok chatbot went on an undressing spree earlier this year. Last month eight states sued OpenAI for a separate set of alleged harms to children, citing lawsuits alleging ChatGPT encouraged illegal substance use and suicide.
OpenAI says its classifier dramatically cuts down on false positives, flagging 48 percent fewer images, while the images it did identify were twice as likely to contain abusive material. It’s designed to catch abusive AI-generated images produced by a variety of tools, including open-source models and nudifying apps. It’s also the first broadly available CSAM classifier with a specific flag for AI-generated material, said OpenAI’s head of child safety public policy, John Buckley, at the briefing. “It’s important for industry to be able to understand what images may contain a fictional child versus a real child,” Buckley added. “That triage is critical in law enforcement reporting flows.” He also emphasized, however, that laws should recognize the harm of AI-generated CSAM: “It potentially erodes social norms in offending against children, and it’s often found colocated with child sexual abuse imagery of real children,” Buckley said.
OpenAI says its classifier dramatically cuts down on false positives, flagging 48 percent fewer images
OpenAI’s own ChatGPT image generator is designed to deny user requests for CSAM. Now, users who attempt to produce it will be shown a new warning developed with expert guidance to try to encourage them to seek help. A first offense will trigger a 24-hour pause in accessing ChatGPT and warn the user their account could be permanently closed, while offering support resources to combat the behavior. OpenAI says it reports “all instances of CSAM” to NCMEC. In a statement, Buckley explained that the 24-hour pause is based on expert advice for best practices “and international evidence on what works to prevent and respond to CSAM seeking vs CSAM generation.” The point is “to interrupt harmful behavior and direct people toward specialist help to stop it.”
Jackson said that North Carolina and many other states now have laws that cover synthetic CSAM, but that partnering with a tech company like OpenAI to help deter its creation is a fairly novel approach to an emerging issue. “Most of what AGs do is accountability work,” he told reporters at the briefing. “Most of our jurisdiction kicks in after the fact to hold people accountable for harm. But with this, we wanted to see if it was possible to develop a model of working together to prevent that harm. And I would say it’s still basically an experiment.”

British actor Robert Pattinson, star of three mega-franchises, "The Batman", "Harry Potter" and "Twilight", has been named as the seventh 007. The announcement ends years of speculation about who would inherit the beloved role from Daniel Craig and comes five years after the last Bond release, "No Time to Die".
Robert Pattinson was unveiled as the next James Bond on Monday, becoming the seventh actor to play the iconic British spy and the first since Amazon MGM took over the beloved film franchise.
The naming of Pattinson comes during the longest hiatus in 007 history and ends years of rampant speculation about who would inherit the role from Daniel Craig. It comes five years after 2021's “No Time to Die,” the first film in Bond’s 64-year history on the silver screen to conclude with the character's death. But 007 will be reborn, yet again, in the 26th Bond film, directed by Denis Villeneuve.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. “... To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”
Read more New James Bond actor expected 'within weeks' as 'unexpected' frontrunners emerge
Pattinson only entered the Bond rumour mill recently after the revelation that he screen-tested for the role. Others reportedly in the mix included Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult.
While producers were long expected to go with a young, less-proven star, they instead opted for one of the best-known actors of his generation. Pattinson, 40, is also relatively old to begin as 007. The actor is currently in production on another iconic role in “The Batman Part II”.
Pattinson comes in already associated with three mega-franchises in “The Batman,” “Twilight” and “Harry Potter”. But since his breakthrough in “Twilight”, Pattinson has worked largely in more independent, auteur-driven films such as “Good Time” with the Safdie brothers, Robert Eggers’ “The Lighthouse” and Bong Joon Ho’s “Mickey 17”. Earlier this year, he drew rave reviews for his villainous performance in Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey”.
“We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin,” the director said in a statement.

The casting comes at a pivotal juncture for the franchise. In 2022, Bond’s longtime studio, MGM, was bought by Amazon for $8.5 billion. After haggling over next steps for 007, producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson relinquished creative control of Bond in 2025. The still-untitled Bond 26 is the first Bond movie since 1962's inaugural “Dr. No” in which a Broccoli didn't handpick the super spy.
Casting a new Bond fell instead to producers Amy Pascal – the former Sony Pictures chief and “Spider-Man” producer – and David Heyman, shepherd of “Harry Potter” and “Paddington”. Steven Knight (“Peaky Blinders,” “Locke”) was brought in to write the script.
Before Craig even departed the role, rumors and odds-making persisted nearly round-the-clock on who would follow in the footsteps of Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig. Idris Elba, for one, has spent half his career deflecting 007 conjecture.
The Bond machine has historically never slowed down. But the 26th installment will follow the longest absence ever for Bond. Given that “No Time to Die” completed principal photography in 2019 (its release was delayed due to the coronavirus pandemic), the lull is even longer.
Some fans are sceptical about the new Amazon-controlled chapter for Bond. Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, has vowed to uphold the franchise's legacy and usher in “the next phase in the legendary 007 for audiences around the world”.
At stake is one of the most lucrative film series in Hollywood , based on Ian Fleming's series of novels. The Bond movies have grossed more than $7 billion worldwide in ticket sales. “No Time to Die” collected $774 million in 2021. The movies also spin out endless other revenue streams, from streaming deals and video games to Aston Martins.
Although some Bond actors came to view the role as a yoke around their necks, it turned Craig into a household name. The British actor wasn't widely known before his casting and, at the time, was derided as the first “blonde Bond”.

David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other big names in tech are raising questions about the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation.
Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO.
At the center of this theory is the reporting from The New York Times that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy. US agencies haven’t confirmed whether this is the case, and President Donald Trump claims he was unaware of any spy allegations. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang set off the events that led to his resignation; s ubsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees at Nvidia , including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were funneling chips to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based company, according to Bloomberg .
David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The New York Times ’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN , which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor ’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying : “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.”
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney said , “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.”
SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole.
More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter , calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”

Nvidia’s board of directors is still focused on an investigation into Huang, CNBC reports.
Nvidia’s board of directors “isn’t considering” having Jensen Huang return as CEO, according to a report from CNBC . A source tells the outlet the board “is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back.”
Since Huang’s resignation last week , tech executives, along with current and former Nvidia employees, have called for his reinstatement. An online petition to bring Huang back as CEO has amassed more than 180,000 signatures , including from major figures like Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad.
President Donald Trump said on Monday that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” for Huang to return to Nvidia. A report from the Financial Times also suggests that Huang floated the idea of returning as CEO with some of his colleagues.
Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. The company has also hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate Huang’s conduct .

After pausing its Level 3 system, Mercedes-Benz is rolling out two new Level 2 driver-assistance features in 2027—starting with a California early access program next month.
Mercedes-Benz is tossing its hat into the partial autonomy ring with the launch of two new features next year : hands-free highway driving and a point-to-point city navigation system. The new features will put the German automaker in competition with Tesla, which is currently leading the auto industry in the development of hands-free systems.
Mercedes’ point-to-point driver assist feature, called MB.Drive Assist Pro, will handle most of the driving on local roads and in dense, urban traffic. Once a destination is plugged into the vehicle’s navigation, the system assists across the entire route, handling highway exits, lane changes, intersections, and traffic lights. But unlike Tesla’s Full Self-Driving, MB.Drive Assist Pro requires that drivers keep their hands on the wheel while navigating through cities.
The system is powered by 27 sensors (10 cameras, 5 radars, 12 ultrasonic sensors) and a high-performance computer capable of 254 TOPS running on the new MB.OS architecture. That computer runs on Nvidia’s Drive AV stack, blending pure AI with a deterministic “Halos” safety guardrail layer. ( We got to experience the point-to-point system as a passenger during a demonstration in San Francisco last year.)
Unlike FSD, MB.Drive Assist Pro requires that drivers keep their hands on the wheel while navigating through cities.
The Hands-Free Highway Assist, meanwhile, works similarly to GM’s Super Cruise or Ford’s BlueCruise, in that drivers are able to take their hands off the steering wheel when driving on approved, controlled-access highways. The highway assist can also handle speeds of up to 85 mph, which is a big jump from Mercedes’ previous generation Drive Pilot’s 40 mph limit. It also includes Proactive Lane Change Assist, which automatically initiates lane changes to pass slower cars or follow navigation toward an exit.
Earlier this month, a number of journalists got to test out the new features in San Francisco. InsideEVs called it a “real challenger” to Tesla FSD, praising how confidently and predictably it handled double-parked trucks, construction zones, and pedestrians during a 25-minute downtown loop. The Drive noted that the system’s “confidence and fluidity” felt more assured than rival systems. And Verge contributor Tim Stevens (writing for Endgadget ) said it handled jaywalkers, cyclists, and sudden U-turns “without issue” and took the stress out of city driving.
Mercedes will begin rolling out both features via an invite-only access program in California next month, ahead of a broader nationwide launch in 2027 — with highway assist arriving in the spring. Eligible vehicles include the CLA Electric, GLC Electric, GLE, GLS, and S-Class, with more vehicles to follow in 2028. While Mercedes hasn’t announced exact pricing yet, eligible owners will be able to unlock the software over the air through the automaker’s online store using one-month, one-year, or three-year subscription plans.
The launch of the new features comes after Mercedes paused development of a Level 3 system , in which drivers can take their eyes off the road, in addition to their hands off the wheel, during certain approved stretches of highway. By pivoting to hands-free highway driving and point-to-point city navigation, Mercedes is betting that its Nvidia-powered, Level 2 features will have more wide appeal — and less regulatory resistance.

Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, new Harvard research has found.
The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability , also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels , and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom.
Federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid. Individual data centers’ power use is often considered proprietary business information, and data center operators and utilities do not have to disclose specific numbers to the public.
The Harvard study specifically focuses on hyperscale data centers—the largest types of facilities, which have become flashpoints in community opposition across the country. While often used for AI inference or training, not all of the hyperscalers surveyed in this study are being used for AI.
“Hyperscalers have been growing fast, even before the AI boom,” says Jon Koomey, an energy researcher who was not a part of the study.
To assemble their dataset, the Harvard researchers put together a list of 403 hyperscale data centers around the country that were operational between May 2024 and April 2025 using a mix of industry research and satellite data. The team then modeled these facilities’ energy use in a variety of scenarios and calculated the energy mix of the regional grids to estimate individual facilities’ carbon emissions. Not all regions were created equal: Data centers in Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—the first of which is home to Data Center Alley—were responsible for more than 50 percent of the energy use in the study.
“Knowing for certain data centers how much they use over a year is a really useful thing,” says Koomey, who notes that a peer-reviewed study is more rigorous than some back-of-the envelope calculations . Koomey has been involved in a regular report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory since 2007 that approximates the energy and water use of the industry. “Sometimes we know it, but sometimes it’s behind an NDA, and no one ever sees it.”
While based on recent data, the study may already be outdated—a reflection of how fast the data center industry is moving. The average size of a facility in the new study is 40 megawatts, which is relatively small compared to some of the data centers under development today. Developers are building campuses that are hundreds or even thousands of megawatts, and there are proposals for still larger data centers.
“Some of the massive campuses being proposed today are substantially larger than the typical facility in our dataset,” says Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard’s T. H. Chan School of Public Health and the lead author of the study.
The study also does not look at developers who choose to build power plants onsite, known as behind-the-meter power—a factor Koomey calls a “wild card” in accurately assessing total data center power use. Plans for behind-the-meter power generation have skyrocketed at proposed data center sites across the US over the past year, with as many as 189 gigawatts in the pipeline earmarked for data centers alone. Many of these plants rely increasingly on inefficient natural gas turbines . BloombergNEF estimated last week that if all of the behind-the-meter power plants in the development queue in the US get built, it could increase overall US emissions by 10 percent.
While the federal government hasn’t tracked data center energy use to date, that could change soon, and it could be a boon to researchers and the public. The Energy Information Agency, the arm of the federal government that tracks energy use across various sectors, conducted three pilot surveys of data center power use across 10 states this year. Those pilot surveys are now complete, EIA spokesperson Lee Tucker tells WIRED, and the agency is currently using them to design a potential voluntary survey for the sector.
